description: CT-RATE is a public dataset comprising 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes (over 14.3 million 2D slices) from 25,692 scans of 21,304 unique patients, paired with corresponding radiology text reports. Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities. The dataset includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital, divided into training and internal validation sets.
name: CT-RATE
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each CT volume is annotated with 18 abnormality labels. The 1,000 manually annotated reports used for training the automated labeler were each labeled for 18 distinct abnormalities.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected Turkish-to-English translations of radiology reports. Radiology reports were originally authored by radiologists at Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. Data anonymization and annotation were managed by team members F.A., A.G.S., S.N.E., and I.D.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: To develop an automated label extractor, 1,000 reports were manually annotated by merging findings and impression sections to create a multi-label dataset identifying 18 abnormalities. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. Similar conditions were grouped (e.g., left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction; various lung opacities under lung opacity; lung and fissural nodules as lung nodules). The annotated reports were divided into training (80%, 800 reports) and validation (20%, 200 reports) sets. The finetuned RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model was then applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports.
rai:dataBiases: CT-RATE is a single-institution dataset from Istanbul Medipol University, which may introduce geographic and clinical setting biases that limit generalizability to other populations. The dataset originates from a single geographic and clinical setting. An ablation study showed performance increases with larger training sets, suggesting that incorporating data from multiple institutions and more diverse patient populations could further enhance model robustness.
rai:dataCollection: CT-RATE was curated from chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. The dataset includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023, totaling 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. The cohort was divided into 20,000 patients for training and 1,304 for validation. Volumes were reconstructed using various techniques for different window settings. Reports were originally in Turkish and translated to English.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes in various resolutions (512×512, 768×768, 1024×1024 pixels) with varying slice thicknesses (0.035 to 6 mm) and axial pixel spacing (0.227 to 1.416 mm), acquired using Philips, Siemens, and PNMS CT scanners. Corresponding radiology reports were structured into four sections: clinical information, technique, findings, and impression, originally written in Turkish by radiologists.
rai:dataLimitations: CT-RATE is a single-center dataset from one geographic and clinical setting, limiting generalizability. CT-CLIP depends on specific terminology used in reports and prompt choice during zero-shot detection. The dataset is limited to chest CT volumes; other 3D imaging modalities (MRI, PET) and anatomical regions are not included. Report quality remains insufficient for clinical deployment. The current models are limited to chest CT volumes.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: CT volumes were reconstructed using various techniques to suit different window settings (e.g., sharper kernels for lung abnormalities, smoother kernels for mediastinal issues), resulting in multiple reconstructed volumes per CT exam. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model (TotalSegmentator). A VQA dataset of over 2.7 million question-answer pairs was derived from CT-RATE reports using Llama 3.1 8B.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each CT volume was resized to achieve uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in z-axis. Volumes were center-cropped or padded to a consistent resolution of 480×480×240. CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit (HU) values using intercept and slope values from metadata, clipped to -1000 to 1000 HU. During training, values were normalized to -1 to 1. Each volume's orientation was standardized. Volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest were excluded. Reports were anonymized (personal information removed via regular expressions), translated from Turkish to English using Google Translate API, and reviewed by bilingual medical students. All identifying information was removed from metadata.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors plan to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels are already openly available through the CT-RATE repository on Hugging Face.
rai:dataSocialImpact: CT-RATE enables development of AI models for 3D medical imaging that can assist radiologists in diagnosing various abnormalities, reducing workload, and potentially saving lives in situations where immediate radiological expertise is not available. The open-source release addresses critical challenges in 3D medical imaging and lays the groundwork for future innovations in medical AI and improved patient care.
rai:dataUseCases: CT-RATE is intended for training and evaluating AI models for 3D chest CT analysis, including: multi-abnormality detection, case retrieval (volume-to-volume and report-to-volume), radiology report generation, visual question answering (VQA), contrastive language-image pretraining, and development of multimodal AI assistants for 3D medical imaging.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m (finetuned for automated multi-label abnormality classification from radiology reports); Google Translate API (for Turkish-to-English translation of reports); Llama 3.1 8B (for generating VQA question-answer pairs); TotalSegmentator (for organ-level anatomical segmentation labels)
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains medical imaging data (chest CT volumes) and radiology reports. All personal information was anonymized: reports were de-identified by removing patient and medical professional identifiers and date-related information using regular expressions. CT volume metadata was also anonymized by removing all identifying information about patients and medical professionals. Ethical approval was obtained from the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at Istanbul Medipol University.

evidence.name: We introduce CT-RATE, a public dataset that pairs 3D medical images with corresponding textual reports. CT-RATE comprises 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 unique patients.
evidence.description: To address these challenges, we introduce CT-RATE, a dataset that pairs 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes (over 14.3 million 2D slices) from 25,692 scans of 21,304 patients with corresponding radiology reports. Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities, supporting extensive validation and fine-tuning. CT-RATE is fully open-source.

evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The CT volumes are provided in various resolutions: 65.4% in 512×512 px, 4.2% in 768×768 px, and 30.4% in 1024×1024 px. The radiology reports are structured into four sections: clinical information, technique, findings, and impression.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: First, each volume is resized to achieve uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis. The CT volumes are then either center-cropped or padded to reach a consistent resolution of 480×480×240, ensuring comprehensive inclusion of the patient's relevant area for the interpretation. Subsequently, we convert each CT volume to Hounsfield Unit (HU) values using intercept and slope values from the metadata. HU values, a measure of radiodensity, are clipped to a range of -1000 to 1000.

evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Leveraging this dataset, we finetune the RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model [34], which was originally trained on over 4 million radiology reports. Then, we apply it to classify the remaining 24,692 reports.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities, supporting extensive validation and fine-tuning.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned model's precision, recall, and F1 scores, detailed in Supplementary Table2, show robust classification across abnormalities, ensuring the CT-RATE dataset is enriched with high-quality labels.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: First, biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence our self-supervised training. Although we curate a large and diverse set of volume-report pairs, the data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of our models to other populations.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Despite these advancements, our CT-RATE dataset and the CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT models have certain limitations. First, biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence our self-supervised training. Although we curate a large and diverse set of volume-report pairs, the data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of our models to other populations. Finally, our current models are limited to chest CT volumes.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: To uphold patient privacy, we anonymize all chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports before conducting any computational analysis. To anonymize the CT-RATE dataset, we first anonymize reports by removing all personal information pertaining to patients and medical professionals. This process involves targeted searches using regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Collectively, the open-source release of CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT not only addresses critical challenges in 3D medical imaging but also lays the groundwork for future innovations in medical AI and improved patient care.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Leveraging CT-RATE, we develop CT-CLIP, a CT-focused contrastive language-image pretraining framework designed for broad applications without the need for task-specific training. We demonstrate how CT-CLIP can be used in multi-abnormality detection and case retrieval, and outperforms state-of-the-art fully supervised models across all key metrics.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: In clinical practice, CT volumes are reconstructed with various techniques for specific diagnostic requirements. Sharper kernels, for instance, improve resolution for lung abnormalities, whereas smoother kernels are favored for assessing mediastinal issues. For that reason, we incorporate every reconstructed volume from the hospital database into our dataset.
